opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's really one that came out of our day-to-day work. When you look at most of the existing safety taxonomies and benchmarks out there, they were designed with a very general consumer chatbot in mind. So they focus on things like toxicity, hate speech, violent content, self-harm, weapons — categories that matter a lot if you're deploying an open-ended assistant to millions of anonymous users. And those things don't go away in finance, but they're often not where the real risk lives.

In financial services, the harms that actually keep people up at night look quite different. Think about a model that inadvertently gives what amounts to personalized investment advice when it isn't licensed or supposed to, or one that leaks material non-public information, or produces a summary of an earnings call that subtly misstates a number. Think about content that could be read as market manipulation, or something that violates confidentiality obligations between clients, or a response that runs afoul of fair lending or anti-discrimination rules. None of those would typically get flagged by a general-purpose toxicity classifier, because the text itself looks completely benign. It's polite, it's fluent, it's on-topic — and it's still a serious problem.

So part of the argument is just coverage: the general taxonomies have blind spots precisely in the areas that a regulated industry cares most about. But there's a second part, which is about context. Whether something is harmful in finance depends heavily on who the user is, what their role is, what jurisdiction you're in, and what the application is meant to do. The same sentence might be totally fine for an internal analyst and a compliance violation if it goes to a retail customer. A one-size-fits-all taxonomy can't really capture that.

And the third piece is accountability. Financial institutions already operate under well-defined regulatory frameworks, and they need to be able to map AI risks onto the controls and obligations they already have. If your safety categories are vague or borrowed from a different domain, it's very hard to translate them into concrete testing, guardrails, and documentation that a risk or compliance team can actually sign off on. Having a domain-specific taxonomy gives everyone — the model builders, the red teamers, the risk managers — a shared vocabulary that's grounded in how the business actually works.

So the broader point we were trying to make is that "safety" isn't a single universal property of a model. It's always relative to a deployment context, and finance is a really clear example of why you need to define it with that context in mind.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose taxonomies have blind spots in finance and gives examples of financial misconduct and compliance harms that need explicit coverage.

r002.rationale: It mentions leaking material non-public information, but does not identify database connections and conversational queries as the exposure mechanism.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes users and deployment contexts, but does not attribute differing safety priorities to differences in users’ incentives.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. It's great to be here.

So the short answer is that the general-purpose safety taxonomies that most of the field has converged on were built with a very different threat model in mind. If you look at the categories that show up in most model cards or in the big safety benchmarks, you see things like toxicity, hate speech, self-harm, violent content, sexual content, maybe dangerous capabilities around bio or cyber. Those are real and important, and we absolutely care about them. But when you sit down with the people who actually run risk and compliance at a financial institution and ask them what keeps them up at night about deploying a language model, that list is almost never what they bring up first.

What they bring up is things like: is the model going to give something that looks like financial advice to a retail customer when we're not licensed to do that in this channel? Is it going to leak material non-public information that it picked up from an internal document into a summary that goes to someone who shouldn't see it? Is it going to confidently state a figure about a company's earnings that's just wrong, and someone acts on it? Is it going to produce something that reads as a recommendation when it should be purely descriptive? Those are the failure modes that create actual regulatory and legal exposure, and they basically don't appear in the general taxonomies at all.

And the inverse is also true. A lot of the things that a general-purpose safety filter would flag as problematic are completely routine in a financial context. Talking about bankruptcy, fraud, insider trading, money laundering, market manipulation, those are all topics a compliance analyst or a research analyst needs to discuss every single day. If your safety layer is tuned on a general consumer taxonomy, you end up with a system that refuses to help with core workflows while letting through the stuff that actually matters to the business. So you get both false positives and false negatives in exactly the wrong places.

The other piece is that the harms in finance are often very subtle and very domain-dependent. Whether a particular statement is problematic can hinge on who the audience is, what jurisdiction you're in, whether the information is public, what the product is. A single sentence can be perfectly fine in an internal research note and a serious problem if it's shown to a retail client. A general taxonomy just doesn't have the resolution to capture that. You need categories that are grounded in how the industry actually thinks about risk, things like suitability, confidentiality, fiduciary obligations, and the specific rules around disclosure.

So when we started looking at this, the motivation really was: we don't think the existing frameworks are wrong, we think they're incomplete for this setting. And if you want to actually evaluate whether a model is safe to deploy in a bank or an asset manager, you need a taxonomy that reflects the risks that organization is actually accountable for. Otherwise you're measuring the wrong thing and calling it safety.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose filters may flag routine financial discussions such as fraud and insider trading, but it does not argue that financial misconduct deserves more explicit emphasis in financial-services taxonomies.

r002.rationale: It describes possible leakage of material nonpublic information from an internal document into a summary, but does not identify database connections or conversational queries as the exposure mechanism.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts financial risk and compliance concerns with general-purpose safety priorities, but does not attribute that difference to users’ incentives.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that safety depends on the context in which a model is used. A general-purpose taxonomy might tell you whether an answer contains harmful content, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it’s appropriate in a financial setting. An answer can sound perfectly reasonable and still mislead someone about risk or give advice that isn’t suitable for their circumstances.

And financial services covers very different applications. Summarizing a document for an analyst is different from answering a customer’s question about a loan or helping someone make an investment decision. You have to consider who’s using the system, what information it has access to, and what consequences its output could have.

So a specialized taxonomy helps make those distinctions explicit. It connects broad concerns—things like accuracy, privacy, and fairness—to concrete failure modes that you can evaluate and build safeguards around. The goal is to move from ‘Is this model safe?’ to ‘Is this system safe enough for this particular use?’

r001.rationale: It says general-purpose taxonomies may miss financial-context risks, but does not identify financial misconduct or argue for emphasizing it more explicitly.

r002.rationale: It mentions information access generally, but not databases with nonpublic information or exposure through conversational queries.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes types of users and applications, but does not attribute safety-priority differences to users’ incentives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that safety really depends on the context in which a model is being used. A general-purpose taxonomy might cover things like harmful content, bias, or privacy, and those are all relevant to financial services. But they don’t fully capture what can go wrong in a financial application.

For example, a response can be perfectly polite and contain no obviously harmful content, but still give misleading financial advice or make an unsupported claim about a product. Whether that response is appropriate also depends on who’s receiving it and what the system is authorized to do. Explaining an investment concept is a different task from recommending an investment to a particular customer.

So you need a taxonomy that connects those broad safety concerns to specific use cases and consequences. That gives you something concrete to evaluate: what failures are we looking for, how serious are they, and what safeguards do we need? The general-purpose categories are a useful starting point, but the domain context is what makes them actionable.

r001.rationale: It mentions misleading financial advice and unsupported product claims, but does not argue that financial misconduct needs more explicit emphasis than in general-purpose taxonomies.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss database connections, nonpublic information, or disclosure through conversational queries.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes users and authorized tasks, but does not attribute differing safety priorities to users’ incentives.
